full_query: How do I know if its a canker sore versus herpes

shared_context.condition: aphthous stomatitis and herpes simplex virus infection

sentences: To distinguish between a canker sore (aphthous stomatitis) and herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection, several clinical features can be considered
Aphthous Stomatitis: Typically occurs on non-keratinized mucosal surfaces like the inside of the lips, cheeks, the floor of the mouth, and the soft palate
Herpes Simplex Virus: Often affects keratinized mucosal surfaces such as the gingiva (gums), the hard palate, and the lips (herpes labialis)
Aphthous Stomatitis: Presents as a round or oval ulcer with a yellow or white center and a red border
Herpes Simplex Virus: Begins as grouped vesicles that rupture to form painful ulcers
The lesions may crust over if on the lips
Aphthous Stomatitis: Often recurrent without a clear trigger, although stress, trauma, and certain foods can exacerbate them
Herpes Simplex Virus: Recurrences often triggered by factors such as fever, stress, sunlight, or immunosuppression
Aphthous Stomatitis: Typically does not have prodromal symptoms
Herpes Simplex Virus: Often preceded by prodromal symptoms such as tingling, itching, or pain in the area before the appearance of lesions
Aphthous Stomatitis: Painful, with ulcers lasting from 7 to 14 days and healing without scarring
Herpes Simplex Virus: Painful, with lesions healing over 2 to 4 weeks
Recurrent lesions tend to heal faster
Aphthous Stomatitis: Usually not associated with systemic symptoms
Herpes Simplex Virus: Primary infection may be accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, and lymphadenopathy
